title: What AI Disclosure Means
body:
AI disclosure means telling an audience, plainly, where machine assistance shaped a piece of content. It matters because audiences judge content differently when they know how it was made: a photograph presented as a witness record carries different weight from an image made by a generator, and advice presented as a person's judgement carries different weight from text drafted by a model. Disclosure does not apologise for using a tool; it lets the audience judge the result with full information.

Method. Disclose the role the machine played, in the place the audience will see it, using words the audience understands. A disclosure that is technically true but hidden, vague, or written in jargon fails its purpose, since the audience cannot act on information it cannot find or parse. Keep the disclosure with the content wherever the content travels, not only on the page where it first appeared.

Checklist.

  • Name the machine's role plainly
  • Place disclosure where audiences see it
  • Use words audiences understand
  • Keep disclosure with travelling content
  • Disclosure informs, it does not apologise

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for What AI Disclosure Means. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: machine role: drafted text; disclosure good: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not use disclosure as a shield for misleading content: labelling a false claim as machine-made does not make the claim true, and the creator remains responsible for what they publish. Disclosure and accuracy are separate duties, and both must be met. title: Visible Labels: Where a Label Belongs
body:
A label that cannot be found is not a label. For images, the label belongs on or beside the image; for video, at the start and in the description; for audio, in the spoken introduction or the show notes where listeners look; for text, at the top or beside the byline. Placement follows attention: the label must meet the audience at the moment they form their first impression, not after they have already judged the content as human-made.

Method. Place the label in the same frame as the content's first impression, repeat it in the description or caption where the format allows, and keep it legible at the size the content is usually viewed. For short-form content that is reshared without captions, put the label inside the media itself, since a caption-only label is lost on the first reshare. Test placement by showing the content to a fresh reader and asking what they believe about its origin.

Checklist.

  • Label meets the first impression
  • Repeat in description where possible
  • Legible at usual viewing size
  • Inside the media for reshare-prone formats
  • Test with a fresh reader

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Visible Labels: Where a Label Belongs. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: formats labelled: 3; image label: on image; all placed: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not place the label only in a settings page, a footnote nobody opens, or a hashtag buried among many, since those placements hide disclosure while claiming it. A label that requires effort to find will be found only by people who already suspected the truth. title: Disclosure Wording Audiences Understand
body:
Disclosure wording fails when it uses terms the audience does not share, such as model names, technical processes, or legal phrases. Audiences understand plain sentences about what happened: this image was generated by a machine from a text description, this article was drafted by a machine and checked by a person, this voice was synthesised from a script. Wording should name the actor, the action, and the human check, in that order, so the audience can judge the result.

Method. Write disclosures as one plain sentence naming what the machine did and what a person did afterwards, and use the same wording across a creator's work so audiences learn to recognise it. Avoid words that minimise the machine's role, such as merely assisted, where the machine in fact generated the content, and avoid words that exaggerate a human check that did not happen. Test wording on a non-specialist reader before publishing it widely.

Checklist.

  • One plain sentence
  • Machine role, then human check
  • Same wording across a creator's work
  • No minimising words for generation
  • Test on a non-specialist reader

Use and limits. Do not write a disclosure that is technically accurate but misleading in emphasis, such as crediting a human editor for work the machine generated wholesale. The test is what an ordinary reader takes away, not what a careful lawyer could defend. title: Provenance Metadata: What Travels With a File
body:
Provenance metadata is information embedded in or attached to a file that records how the file was made, edited, and published, so the history travels with the file rather than living only on the original page. Standards for content credentials attach a signed record of creation and edits to images and other media, letting a viewer check the file's history where the viewing tool supports it. Metadata does not prove a file is true; it proves what is claimed about how the file was made, which is a narrower and more honest claim.

Method. Preserve provenance by keeping original files and their metadata through editing, using tools that retain content credentials where available, and checking that exports and uploads have not stripped the record. Explain provenance to audiences in plain words alongside any technical record, since a cryptographic record no audience member can read does not inform them. Where a tool strips metadata, add a visible label instead, so the loss of provenance does not become a loss of disclosure.

Checklist.

  • Keep originals and metadata through editing
  • Use tools that retain credentials where available
  • Check exports have not stripped the record
  • Explain provenance in plain words
  • Visible label where metadata is stripped

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Provenance Metadata: What Travels With a File. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: history steps: 3; history complete: True; first step: created Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not present provenance as proof of truth: a file with a complete history can still depict a staged scene, and a file with no history can still be genuine. Provenance answers how, not whether, and confusing the two misleads audiences in a new way. title: Watermarking: Visible, Invisible, and Their Limits
body:
Watermarking marks machine-made content so it can be recognised later: visible watermarks are seen by audiences, invisible watermarks are embedded in the data and detected by tools, and both are sometimes combined. Visible marks inform audiences directly but can be cropped or covered; invisible marks survive ordinary resharing better but inform no one unless a tool checks for them. Neither is permanent against a determined remover, and neither replaces a visible label for the audience in front of the work.

Method. Use visible labels for audience disclosure and invisible marks as a backstop for detection where the generating tool provides them, and do not rely on either alone. Tell audiences what the marks mean where they matter, test whether ordinary edits such as cropping, compression, or screenshots remove the marks, and keep the visible label even where an invisible mark exists, since the audience in front of the work cannot see the invisible one.

Checklist.

  • Visible label for the audience
  • Invisible mark as detection backstop
  • Test against cropping and compression
  • Keep the visible label regardless
  • Explain what marks mean

title: Disclosing Degrees: Help, Editing, and Generation
body:
Machine involvement is not one thing: a machine may correct spelling, suggest a sentence, draft a whole article, or generate an image from nothing, and audiences judge those degrees differently. Disclosure should match the degree, naming the largest role the machine actually played rather than the smallest role that can be defended. A work that was machine-drafted and human-edited should not be disclosed as merely machine-assisted, since the audience's judgement depends on knowing the draft itself was machine-made.

Method. Grade the machine's role honestly: assistance for small corrections and suggestions, drafting for substantial machine-written or machine-drawn content later edited by a person, and generation for content the machine produced wholesale from a prompt. Disclose the highest grade that applies, describe the human check that followed, and use the same grades across a creator's work so audiences learn what each grade means in practice.

Checklist.

  • Assistance: small corrections and suggestions
  • Drafting: substantial machine content, human-edited
  • Generation: wholesale machine production
  • Disclose the highest grade that applies
  • Same grades across a creator's work

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Disclosing Degrees: Help, Editing, and Generation. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: role grade: 2; disclose as: drafting; highest grade: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not split a machine's role into small pieces to claim a lower grade, such as calling a machine-drafted article assisted because a person changed some words. The grade follows the substance of the work, not the number of edits made afterwards. title: Disclosure by Medium: Image, Audio, Video, Text
body:
Each medium hides machine involvement differently, so disclosure must adapt to the medium rather than using one form everywhere. Images hide generation behind realism, audio hides synthesis behind a familiar voice, video hides editing behind smooth motion, and text hides drafting behind fluent prose. The disclosure for each medium should meet the audience where that medium deceives: on the image, in the audio's introduction, at the video's start, and beside the text's byline.

Method. For images, label on or beside the image and in the caption; for audio, state the synthesis in the introduction and show notes; for video, label at the start and in the description, and name any synthetic voice or face; for text, state the machine's role beside the byline and describe the human check. In every medium, keep the disclosure with excerpts and clips, since excerpts travel further than full works and carry the deception risk with them.

Checklist.

  • Images: label on image and in caption
  • Audio: state synthesis in introduction
  • Video: label at start and description
  • Text: role beside the byline
  • Disclosure travels with excerpts

Use and limits. Do not disclose in one medium and leave a repurposed version undisclosed in another, such as labelling a video while leaving its audio track, shared alone, without a label. The disclosure follows the content across media, not just across copies. title: Disclosure in News, Research, and Education
body:
News, research, and education are trust-sensitive contexts, where audiences rely on content to make decisions, cite findings, or learn facts, and where undisclosed machine involvement does more damage than in entertainment. In these contexts disclosure must be fuller: not only that a machine was involved, but what it did, what sources it used where relevant, and what human verification followed. A newsroom, a researcher, or a teacher who hides machine involvement risks the trust their whole work depends on.

Method. Disclose the machine's role, the human verification, and, for factual claims, the sources a person checked, in the same place the audience meets the work. Keep a record of prompts, outputs, and checks for factual work, so errors can be traced and corrected, and correct disclosed errors publicly with the same prominence as the original. Where an institution has a disclosure policy, follow it and note it, so audiences see a consistent standard rather than individual improvisation.

Checklist.

  • Machine role, human check, and checked sources
  • Record of prompts, outputs, and checks
  • Errors corrected with equal prominence
  • Institutional policy followed and noted
  • Consistent standard across work

Use and limits. Do not present machine-generated factual claims as researched findings, and do not use disclosure to excuse publishing unchecked claims in a trust-sensitive context. In these contexts, disclosure without verification is still a failure of the work. title: When Disclosure Is Required: Checking the Rules
body:
Disclosure requirements come from several places at once: the platform where content is published, the publisher or employer behind it, contracts with clients or sponsors, and laws that differ by place and by content type. No single checklist covers all of them, so the creator's job is to check each layer before publishing rather than assuming one layer's rules satisfy the others. A disclosure that satisfies a platform may still breach a contract, and a disclosure that satisfies a contract may still miss a legal duty.

Method. Before publishing, check the platform's current disclosure rules, the publisher's or employer's policy, any contract terms, and the general legal duties that apply to the content's type and place, such as advertising or election rules where relevant. Record what was checked and where the disclosure was placed, and recheck when republishing in a new place, since a new platform or jurisdiction can bring new duties. Where the rules are unclear, disclose more rather than less, and seek advice for high-stakes content.

Checklist.

  • Platform rules checked
  • Publisher or employer policy checked
  • Contract terms checked
  • Legal duties for type and place checked
  • Rechecked on republication

title: Correcting a Missing Disclosure
body:
A missing disclosure discovered after publication should be corrected, not hidden, because audiences who learn of machine involvement from others will trust the creator less than audiences who learn it from the creator. A good correction adds the disclosure where the audience will see it, explains briefly that it was missing, and keeps the correction visible rather than quietly editing it into the original without a note. Late honesty repairs more trust than silent perfection ever would.

Method. Add the disclosure to the work itself and to its description, note briefly that the disclosure was added after publication and why, and apply the same correction to copies and excerpts where the creator controls them. Where the work was already widely shared without disclosure, publish the correction in the same place and with similar prominence, so the correction reaches a comparable audience. Review how the disclosure was missed, and fix the workflow step that lost it.

Checklist.

  • Add disclosure to work and description
  • Note it was added after publication
  • Correct controlled copies and excerpts
  • Similar prominence for wide sharing
  • Fix the workflow step that lost it

Do not blame the audience for noticing, and do not delete the work to avoid the correction unless the work itself is harmful, since deletion removes the record the correction would have repaired. title: AI-Edited Versus AI-Generated Work
body:
The line between editing and generation matters because audiences judge them differently: editing polishes work a person substantially made, while generation creates work a person prompted but did not substantially write, draw, or perform. A disclosure should therefore state which side of the line the work falls on, and where a work mixes both, it should state the mix plainly rather than choosing the more flattering label. The test is substance: who supplied the content's ideas, structure, and expression, not merely who touched it last.

Method. Ask what the person supplied: if the person supplied the ideas, structure, and most expression, and the machine polished language or layout, disclose editing. If the machine supplied substantial content from a prompt and the person edited it, disclose generation with editing. If the work mixes sections, disclose the mix section by section where that is practical, and by the highest degree where it is not, so the audience is never given a lower degree than the truth.

Checklist.

  • Who supplied ideas, structure, expression
  • Machine polish means editing
  • Machine substance means generation
  • Mixed work disclosed as a mix
  • Highest degree where sections cannot be split

Use and limits. Do not label machine-generated work as edited merely because a person reviewed it, since review is not authorship, and do not label human work as generated merely because a machine checked its spelling. Either error misleads the audience about who actually made the work. title: Audience Trust: What Hidden Disclosure Costs
body:
Hidden disclosure costs trust in a way that is hard to recover, because the audience's discovery reframes everything the creator has published: if this work hid its machine role, the audience reasonably wonders what else was hidden. The cost falls not only on the individual work but on the creator's whole body of work, and on other creators in the same field, whose honest disclosures are doubted because hidden ones were found. Disclosure is therefore not a cost paid per work, but an investment in the creator's standing across all works.

Method. Treat disclosure as part of publication, budgeted in time like editing or fact-checking, and measure its effect by audience questions rather than by complaints: audiences who understand a work's making ask better questions about it. When a nondisclosure is discovered, correct it promptly and publicly as the previous record describes, and do not respond to discovery with minimisation, since minimisation converts a disclosure failure into a honesty failure. Build a track record of consistent disclosure, which is the only evidence that the next disclosure will also be honest.

Checklist.

  • Disclosure budgeted like editing
  • Audience questions show understanding
  • Prompt public correction on discovery
  • No minimisation in response
  • Consistent track record across works

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Audience Trust: What Hidden Disclosure Costs. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: works: 10; disclosed: 9; disclosure rate: 0.9 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record describes general trust dynamics, not measured statistics about any creator or audience, and it makes no claim about how any particular audience will react. Trust effects vary by field, audience, and history, and creators should judge their own audiences rather than assuming a universal reaction. title: Disclosure in Advertising and Sponsored Content
body:
Advertising and sponsored content carry two disclosures at once: that the content is advertising or sponsored, and what role a machine played in making it. Both must be visible, since an audience that knows content is sponsored but not that its testimonial voice or image was synthesised judges it on a false basis, and an audience that knows it is machine-made but not that it was paid for judges its independence falsely. The two disclosures sit together, in the same place, in plain words.

Method. Label sponsorship and machine involvement together at the content's first meeting with its audience, using plain words for both, and keep both labels with excerpts and reshares. Do not let a sponsorship disclosure hide inside a machine disclosure or vice versa; each must be findable on its own. Where advertising rules in the relevant place require specific wording or placement, follow those requirements and add the machine disclosure alongside them rather than treating compliance with one as satisfying the other.

Checklist.

  • Sponsorship and machine role labelled together
  • Both in plain words
  • Both at first meeting with audience
  • Each findable on its own
  • Both travel with excerpts

Use and limits. This record is general education, not legal advice about advertising rules, which differ by place and by product and change over time. Creators of advertising content should check the rules that apply to their content and place before publishing. title: AI Voices and Likenesses: Consent and Disclosure
body:
Synthetic voices and likenesses raise disclosure questions that go beyond labelling: a synthesised voice that sounds like a real person, or a face that looks like one, affects that person's reputation and consent even when the content itself is labelled. Disclosure must therefore cover not only that a voice or face was synthesised, but whose likeness it draws on and whether that person agreed. A label that says a voice was synthesised without saying whose voice it imitates leaves the most important question unanswered.

Method. Disclose synthesis, name the likeness source where it is a real person, and state the consent basis in general terms the audience can understand, such as made with the person's agreement or made as an original character not based on a real person. Never synthesise a real person's voice or likeness for endorsement, deception, or intimate content without their clear agreement, and where agreement is uncertain, do not publish. Keep consent records with the work's record, so a later question about consent can be answered from the record rather than from memory.

Checklist.

  • Synthesis disclosed
  • Likeness source named where real
  • Consent basis stated generally
  • No endorsement or deception without agreement
  • Consent records kept with the work

title: Keeping Disclosure Records
body:
Disclosure records let a creator answer later questions about a work's making without relying on memory: what the machine did, what the person checked, where the disclosure was placed, and what changed in each revision. Without a record, a creator who is asked about an old work must reconstruct its making from fragments, and reconstruction under pressure produces confident errors. A short version note written at publication prevents that failure for the cost of a few lines.

Method. Write a version note at publication naming the machine's role, the human check, the disclosure wording and placement, and the date, and add a line for each revision that changes the machine's role or the disclosure. Keep notes with the work or in one searchable place per creator, and consult them before republishing, excerpting, or defending a work. When a work is corrected, the note records the correction and its date alongside the original entry, rather than overwriting it.

Checklist.

  • Version note at publication
  • Machine role, check, wording, placement, date
  • Line per revision changing role or disclosure
  • Notes searchable in one place
  • Corrections added, not overwritten

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Keeping Disclosure Records. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: versions recorded: 2; latest version: 2; latest role: drafted and edited Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not keep disclosure records that contain private information about other people without a reason, and do not treat a record as a substitute for the disclosure itself: the record informs the creator, while the disclosure informs the audience, and both are needed. title: A Disclosure Checklist for Every Publication
body:
A disclosure checklist turns good intentions into reliable practice by asking the same questions before every publication, so disclosure does not depend on remembering it in a busy moment. The checklist covers the machine's role, the grade of involvement, the wording, the placement, the medium's hand, the travelling record, and the rules layers, and a work is not published until every applicable item is checked or honestly marked as not applicable. Checklists work because they are boring: they catch the step that enthusiasm skips.

Method. Run the checklist before publishing: name the machine's role and grade, write the plain-sentence disclosure, place it at the audience's first meeting, add the medium's hand, attach the travelling record, and check the rules layers for the publication place. Mark items that do not apply with a reason rather than leaving them blank, since a blank item hides whether it was considered. File the completed checklist with the version note, so the publication's disclosure can be audited later from its own record.

Checklist.

  • Machine role and grade named
  • Plain-sentence disclosure written
  • Placement at first meeting
  • Medium hand and travelling record added
  • Rules layers checked and filed

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for A Disclosure Checklist for Every Publication. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: items checked: 4 of 5; ready to publish: False; outstanding: ['rules'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Do not treat the checklist as a ritual that can be ticked without doing the work, since a ticked but undone item is worse than an unticked one: it claims a check that never happened. Where an item cannot be completed, delay publication or disclose the gap, rather than ticking past it.
